title: One Transitory Shock After Another
summary: Fed Governor Christopher Waller delivered a speech on April 17, 2026, outlining how the U.S. economy faces a series of supply-side shocks from both the Middle East conflict disrupting energy production and the cumulative effects of import tariffs, which together risk creating more lasting inflation similar to pandemic-era dynamics. He also detailed unprecedented changes in labor supply, with net immigration falling from 2.3 million in 2024 to approximately 400,000 in 2025 and projected near zero in 2026, fundamentally reducing the number of jobs needed to maintain stable unemployment.
key_points: Net immigration declined sharply from 2.3 million in 2024 to approximately 400,000 in 2025, expected near zero in 2026, combined with population aging to halt labor force growth
With zero labor force growth, the number of jobs needed to maintain steady unemployment has fallen from the historical 50,000-150,000/month range to approximately zero
Conflict with Iran disrupted Middle East energy production and transportation, sending global energy prices higher, with uncertainty about whether Strait of Hormuz will reopen
Import tariffs combined with energy shocks create a risk of more lasting inflation increases, similar to the series of supply shocks during the pandemic
Payroll growth has been highly volatile: -17,000 in December, +160,000 in January, -133,000 in February, +178,000 in March
Waller characterizes the labor market as showing 'weakness that leaves it vulnerable,' with low hiring and low separations, and employers hesitant due to demand uncertainty
why_it_matters: Waller, a voting FOMC member, provides a detailed assessment of how structural shifts in labor supply are changing the relationship between payroll growth and economic health. His framing of 'one transitory shock after another' suggests the Fed views recent inflation pressures as potentially persistent rather than quickly fading, which has implications for the timing and pace of any rate adjustments. The speech signals the Fed must now navigate both demand-side weakness and supply-side price shocks simultaneously.
macro_context: The speech describes an economy where Q1 2026 GDP is estimated to grow at a 2.4% annual rate, driven by strong data center construction and business investment offsetting consumer spending softness. The labor market shows paradoxical conditions: unemployment is stable near the longer-term natural rate, but job-finding rates and openings are declining, with longer unemployment durations even as the headline unemployment count remains steady. This creates policy complexity as traditional recession signals (negative payrolls) may no longer reliably indicate economic distress given zero labor force growth.
